(6) Curvature graph: a checkable Evaluate command with a small tool window holding Scale (1 to 1000) and Density (4 to 400 teeth per edge) sliders. It shows combs on the selected edges, or on every curve feature when no edge is selected; teeth point away from the centre of curvature, their length is curvature times scale (clipped at twice the edge's size), and the tips are joined by an outline. The combs are worked out in a background job and drawn as a display overlay; nothing in the document changes, so it is not an undo step. Sampling loops over at most 400 points per edge, which is bounded and is not a mesh. (7) Golden sample results may now carry a body count (`bodies`) for samples that are meant to have several bodies; the golden test checks it (default 1). Samples: `piped_frame` (a 20 mm tube with 2 mm walls around a 120 by 80 mm rectangle, mitred corners) and `chain_along_curve` (two linked 14 by 8 mm links copied 15 times along a gentle rising helix; neighbouring links never touch, with at least 0.39 mm between them).
Status: Default
Reason: PHASE3_SPEC P3.7 and PLAN Phase 3; STEP round trips must keep the volume.

D293: Split for printing (PLAN Phase 3, PHASE3_SPEC P3.9, FDEF_SPEC 5.3.18). (1) Automatic mode cuts the part's box evenly along X, Y and Z into the fewest pieces that each fit the build volume in the part's own orientation; it does not turn pieces to fit better. The default build volume is the generic printer of PLAN section 8 item 16 (220 by 220 by 250 mm) until printer profiles exist; the panel remembers the last values in the session. Planes mode cuts at picked plane features and flat faces (treated as endless). All cuts run as one split operation. A part that already fits gives a warning and is not cut; planes that miss the part are an error. (2) Pins are separate bodies printed on their own: each cut face gets one pin at its area centre, or two at a quarter of its length from the centre when the face is longer than six pin diameters. Both pieces get a hole the clearance wider all round and the clearance deeper than half the pin. A spot needs the hole radius plus 1 mm of material to the face's edge, and the whole hole must lie in material; otherwise it is skipped with a warning naming how many cut faces had no room. (3) Dovetail keys are separate bodies shaped like two dovetails back to back across the seam (flanks at 15 degrees), placed like pins and running across the cut face's short direction, so a key slides in from the side and locks the pieces together. The key is the part's own material inside that shape; the pocket is the shape grown by the clearance. (4) Pieces and connectors stay separate bodies. After an automatic split each piece is checked against the build volume; pins that make a piece too large give a warning. The default clearance is 0.2 mm (the profile fit tolerance will replace it when printer profiles exist). (5) Sample `split_with_pins`: a 300 by 120 by 30 mm block split in two for a 220 mm printer with two 5 mm pins.
Status: Default
Reason: PLAN Phase 3; the simplest cuts that always fit, with connectors that print without supports.

D294: Mesh import (PLAN Phase 3, PHASE3_SPEC P3.9, FDEF_SPEC 5.3.19). (1) File, Open accepts `.stl`, `.3mf` and `.obj` and makes a new part with the mesh; Insert, Import Mesh adds one to the open part in one undoable step (block and feature together, as D290). The file is embedded as a `mesh` block with its `format`. (2) Readers use whole array operations only (CLAUDE.md 5A rule 2): binary STL is read straight into a numpy record array; ASCII STL is split into tokens and the numbers after each `vertex` taken with one index array; OBJ vertices and triangle and quad faces are matched with one regular expression each over the whole file (faces with more than four corners are fanned line by line, which is rare); 3MF vertices and triangles are matched per object with one regular expression each, build item transforms are applied with one matrix product, and the model unit is honoured. 3MF components and OBJ texture or normal indices are ignored. STL and OBJ have no unit and are read as millimetres. Shared corners are merged with one `numpy.unique`, and triangles with a repeated corner or no area are dropped. A mesh is kept as float32 vertices and int32 triangles (PLAN 11.4 item 5). (3) A mesh is a reference body by default: it is drawn as a face carrying only its triangles (handed to the kernel as binary STL, so no Python loop builds it) and is not part of the solid, so it adds no body. Above 100,000 triangles the feature has a warning, shown in the status bar after import. (4) Convert to Solid (a tick box in the feature's panel) runs only when asked: the kernel reads the triangles as faces, sews them at 0.000001 mm, makes a solid from each closed shell and merges coplanar triangles into one face. A mesh with holes is an error that suggests repairing it or keeping it as a reference. The converted solid is a separate body unless Merge with the part is ticked, so it can be used by later features and by the multibody tools. (5) Not built here: measuring and sectioning a reference mesh belong to the measure and section view tools of other work packages; the numpy mesh is kept in the feature result (`extras["mesh"]`) for them. The PLAN line stays open until they exist. (6) Sample `imported_mesh_with_cut`: a box mesh written in code, converted to a solid, with a slot cut through it.
Status: Default
Reason: PLAN Phase 3 and CLAUDE.md 5A; meshes stay meshes unless the user asks.

D250: Model geometry snapping (docs/GAP_REPORT.md WP14, TOOL_SPEC T1.2.2, T3.1 note 3, T3.2.1, D116 item 3, owner note 1). (1) When a sketch opens, a worker thread projects the part along the sketch normal (`core/sketch/projection.py`): every vertex, every straight edge, every round edge whose axis is along the normal (with its centre), and the part origin. Edges seen at a slant (ellipses) and other curves are drawn only. Items that land on the same spot keep the one nearest the sketch plane. The part is the one the sketch sees: before the sketch for an existing sketch, the finished part for a new one. The result is kept for the last four opened sketches, keyed by the part's rebuild key and the plane, and never recomputed per mouse move. (2) Snap targets and their rank in the T1.2.3 order: part vertices and the origin with end points, revealed round edge centres with centres (hover reveal, W3.2, as before), straight edge midpoints with midpoints, and points on straight and round edges with on curve. Sketch items win a tie. Lookups are whole array numpy queries (`ui/sketch_tools/model_snap.py`). Model vertices are not alignment guide sources, to keep guides readable on large parts. (3) Snapping adds the matching relation to a fixed construction copy, reused when one is already there: a point for vertices, centres and the origin (Coincident), a line for straight edges (Coincident on the line, or Midpoint), a circle for round edges (Coincident on the circle). Points on other curves snap without a relation. Smart Dimension picks the copy; a drag dropped on a vertex, centre or edge midpoint gets the relation under the D124 item 3 rules. The projected part origin of a face sketch is the sketch origin itself, which gets no source. (4) Each copy remembers its source by persistent name in an optional `source` key (FDEF_SPEC 6 item 9). A sketch with sources is rebuilt when the part before it changes (new `FeatureType.reads_body`). The rebuild resolves each source by name only, with no position fallback (a copy is already a position snapshot), and compares it with the copy within 1e-6 mm. A moved source gives a warning with an "Update Copies" fix button that carries the new positions; a source that no longer resolves gives a warning with no fix. (5) Update never runs on its own (CLAUDE.md rule 12): in the sketch editor a bar at the top lists the out of date and lost copies with an Update button (one step on the sketch's undo list); in the errors panel the fix moves the copies, solves the sketch so tied geometry follows, and is one undoable document command. Lost copies stay where they are.
Status: Default
Reason: The spec asks for snaps to projected model geometry and a warning instead of silent stale copies, but not how sources are named, when the check runs or what Update does to tied geometry. Names reuse the existing edge and vertex grammar, and an optional key keeps older files unchanged.

D251: Reference geometry (docs/PHASE2_SPEC.md P2.10, PLAN Phase 2). (1) Four feature types, one module each in `core/features`: `ref_plane` (offset, angle, three points, normal to curve, mid plane, parallel through a point), `ref_axis` (line, two planes, two points, cylinder axis, point and face normal), `ref_point` (arc centre, face centre, intersection, projection, along curve by distance or percent, on a point, X Y Z values) and `coord_system` (origin and directions, or X then Y then Z rotations). Storage is in FDEF_SPEC 5.3.20: a `method` and up to three picks `refs.first` to `refs.third`. The method is guessed from the kinds of the picks until the user chooses one, as P2.10 item 3 asks; a pick's kind is read from its stored snapshot or feature type, so guessing needs no kernel. (2) Not built, as Later: Project onto a curved face, Parallel to screen, Tangent to a curved face, a number of planes or points in one feature, and Mid plane between faces that are not parallel (it is an error that says so). Mid plane, angle and three point planes are enough for the PLAN list. (3) A reference feature result carries a new `FeatureResult.datum` (kind, origin, direction, X direction, length). Reference planes also set `FeatureResult.plane`, so sketches sit on them with the existing `refs.plane` feature form and the plane picker and tree Sketch item offer them. Later reference features can pick earlier ones. Picking them as references for solid features waits for those features' own panels (other work packages). (4) The panel shows OK enabled only when every needed pick is filled, the values are valid and a preview built on a worker thread without an error (P2.10 item 1 "fully defined"); the message line says what is still missing or the build error. The preview draws in the preview colour (D119 item 5) through a new `show_preview_marks` of the 3D view. (5) Display: reference planes are drawn like shown planes (T13 look) but show until hidden on purpose, through the existing `appearance.hidden` list (FDEF_SPEC 10 item 4), with Hide or Show in the tree menu and H. Axes are drawn as a line through the part (or the picked edge's length), points as a small cross and coordinate systems as three short axes, with the finished sketch lines, so no new 3D view layer is needed. Hide All Reference Geometry (Ctrl+H) hides them too. (6) Default names are "Plane 1", "Axis 1", "Point 1" and "Coordinate System 1" (D110 item 4). The four commands are in the Features tab in a Reference Geometry group and in the Insert menu, with no default keys.
Status: Default
Reason: P2.10 lists many constraint choices; this builds the PLAN Phase 2 list plus the cheap, common extras, keeps one module per type, and uses existing visibility and plane drawing so older files and the plane tests stay unchanged.

D252: Measure tool (docs/PHASE2_SPEC.md P2.12, PLAN Phase 2). (1) `core/measure.py` holds the maths, no Qt; the Measure box and the status bar run it on a worker thread and show only the newest answer (CLAUDE.md rule 2). Results are rows with a fixed key, so the box, its history and the status bar read the same. (2) One item: a vertex gives its point; an edge its length, and for a round edge also radius, diameter and centre; a face its area and perimeter (all its edges), and for a cylinder also radius and diameter. Two items: the smallest distance (kernel distance between shapes) with dX, dY, dZ between the two nearest points, and the angle between straight edges or flat faces, between 0 and 90 degrees (a line against a plane gives its angle to the plane). Two circles or arcs: center to center always, plus minimum (shape distance) or maximum (center distance plus both radii, exact for circles in one plane). Three to six items: the smallest distance between any two, total length of the edges and total area of the faces. (3) Options are for the box only and not saved: units (part units, mm or in) and decimals (2 by default), how circles are measured, Show dX dY dZ, XYZ from the part origin or a coordinate system feature (P2.10), and Projected on none or a plane (default or reference plane), which adds the projected and normal distance and the projected area of flat faces. (4) Picks: a click adds the item (up to six; the oldest drops out), clicking a picked item again removes it, an empty click clears all. A Pause tick box stands in for "right click Select pauses measuring", because the right click menu of the 3D view belongs to another work package. Pin keeps the box on top. Closing the box ends the tool; the Measure command toggles it. A rebuild clears the picks, since picked shapes belong to the old part (as the selection does). (5) History: each new result is added at the top for the session; each value row has a Copy button. (6) Status bar (P2.12 item 5): with up to six items selected and no tool needed, the length, area, radius, distance or angle follows the selection count text. (7) Later, not built: callouts in the 3D view, Point to point mode, projection on the screen, projected area of curved faces.
Status: Default
Reason: P2.12 lists the behaviour but not the exact rows, the angle range or how maximum is found. These choices are exact for the common cases and keep kernel work off the UI thread.

D253: Section view (docs/PHASE2_SPEC.md P2.13, PLAN Phase 2). (1) The section is drawn with the 3D viewer's clipping planes and caps, not by cutting the part, so it is display only, needs no kernel work while it changes, and is never saved or put on the undo list (like the display style, D120 item 3). It is a view state of each open part that stays on until turned off (P2.13 item 4). (2) Each section plane removes the material on its normal side. With two or three planes the planes form one chain, so only the region in front of all of them is cut away (a corner cut away view). The rule is `core/section.py`; a test probes the viewer's clipping chain without a GPU to check that it hides exactly that region. (3) A plane starts from Front, Top or Right (buttons and list), a plane of the part (default or reference plane), or the flat face selected when the command started. The offset moves it along its normal, then it turns about its own X and then Y axis, then Reverse flips which side is removed. Offsets are measured from the reference only; "from the picked plane" is the same thing here, since the reference is the picked plane. Section 1 can instead turn about a reference axis, or the round face or straight edge selected when the command started, by an angle. (4) Options: Show section cap (off: see inside), each plane's cap colour (Section 1's colour is the cap colour of the whole chain, because the viewer caps a chain in one colour), and Keep cap color after closing (off: the colour goes back to the default orange when the panel closes with OK). (5) The command `view.section` (no default key) is in the View menu, the view toolbar and the Evaluate tab. It opens the panel; OK keeps the section on, Cancel or the command again turns it off. (6) Later, not built: the transform handle in the 3D view that drags the offset and turns the plane. The fields do the same; the handle needs native view work that cannot be tested without a GPU.
Status: Default
Reason: Viewer clipping keeps the section off the geometry and fast while it changes; the chain rule matches a cut away view, and probing the clip planes keeps the rule tested on CI without a GPU.

D254: Appearance (docs/PHASE2_SPEC.md P2.11, PLAN Phase 2). (1) Storage (FDEF_SPEC 10 item 7): the schema 1 keys `part_color` and `faces` plus two optional maps, `features` (feature id) and `bodies` (body number in Solid Bodies order, since bodies have no persistent names yet). Body numbers can change when bodies are added or merged; a colour on a body then follows the number, which is why feature and face colours are offered first. Face colours that no longer resolve are kept and ignored (FDEF_SPEC 10 item 3). (2) The most specific colour wins: face, feature, body, part (P2.11 item 1); `core/appearance.py` works it out from face names, with no kernel work beyond one face map. (3) A colour change is one undoable command (`SetAppearance`) that redraws the part and the tree but needs no rebuild, like showing or hiding a sketch (D114). (4) Commands, no default keys, in the Edit menu: Appearance (a panel in the left panel: the target list holds the selected faces, the solid feature selected in the tree, each body when there are several, and the part; twelve original swatches, More Colors for the system colour dialog, Remove Color, and the colours in use), Copy Appearance (the shown colour of the first target: the face's own, else its feature's, else the part colour) and Paste Appearance (onto the first target, or the part with nothing selected). (5) The tree's Appearances row (P2.11 item 1) sits under the Solid Bodies folder, so the L4 order of the part, bodies, planes and origin rows stays; it lists each colour with what carries it, and a double click opens the panel. (6) The 3D view draws per face colours with a coloured shape presentation. STEP export writes the part colour and face colours through the kernel's document writer (generic colour on the part, surface colours on faces) only when colours are set beyond the default; otherwise it writes as before. 3MF writes one base material per colour and a material index per triangle; the faces of one colour are meshed together, so there are no Python loops over triangles (CLAUDE.md 5A item 2).
Status: Default
Reason: P2.11 asks for these levels and exports but leaves storage open. Optional maps keep older files byte for byte; feature colours survive edits through face names, which bodies cannot yet.

D310: Hole Tool size tables (PHASE4_SPEC P4.1, CLAUDE.md 7.6). (1) Compiled in `core/features/hole_data.py` from the published standards only: ISO 261 and 262 coarse pitches with tap drill = nominal minus pitch; ISO 273 fine, medium and coarse clearance as Close, Normal and Loose; ISO 4762 socket head diameters (head height equal to the nominal size), ISO 10642 countersunk heads (90 degrees, theoretical diameter) and ISO 4032 nuts; ANSI B1.1 UNC sizes plus #10-32 and 1/4-28 with 75 percent thread tap drills, ASME B18.2.8 close and normal clearance (loose is normal plus 1/32 inch), ASME B18.3 socket and 82 degree flat heads and ASME B18.2.2 nuts. (2) Counterbore diameter is the head diameter plus 1 mm below M12 and 2 mm from M12 (1/16 and 1/8 inch for inch sizes); counterbore depth is the head height. Tapped holes default to a thread of twice the nominal size and a hole three pitches deeper. (3) Heat set insert sizes are typical published values (M2 to M8, #4-40 to 1/4-20), editable in a table kept in the preferences. (4) The panel fills the stored lengths from the tables when the type, standard, size, fit or purpose changes; the feature stores the lengths, so a file rebuilds the same when the tables change. The user can type over any value.
Status: Default
Reason: CLAUDE.md 7.6 asks for standard data compiled from the standards; storing lengths keeps old files stable.

D311: Printing fit presets and the printer fit tolerance (PLAN Phase 4). (1) The fit tolerance is the gap per side a printed part needs to slide freely. Clearance adds twice the tolerance to every hole diameter (and to nut flats and height), Slip once, Press nothing (printed at nominal size so it grips). (2) No printer profile editor exists yet (PLAN Phase 2 work in another session), so the tolerance is kept under `printer/fit_tolerance` in the preferences (default 0.2 mm, D31: profiles are preferences) and copied into the hole's `fit_tolerance` when a fit is chosen, so the file rebuilds the same on any machine. (3) Offset face is a Phase 3 feature not built yet; the fit presets reach it when it lands, so the PLAN item stays open.
Status: Default
Reason: PHASE4_SPEC P4.1 item 5; D31 keeps profiles out of the file but geometry must not change with preferences.

D312: Hole positions and placement (PHASE4_SPEC P4.1 items 3 and 4). (1) The hole's own position sketch is kept inside the hole (`data.positions`, points only, on `refs.plane`) instead of a separate sketch feature, so the preview, OK, Cancel and undo work on one feature and deleting the hole removes its points. Its points are placed by clicking on the face while the Positions tab is open and dimensioned by typing their X and Y in the points table; opening it in sketch mode with snaps, inference lines and dimensions is left out for now (sketch mode only edits sketch features). (2) An existing sketch is used through `refs.sketch`; tick boxes choose points on their own, end points and centres. Deleting such a hole asks whether to keep the sketch, as for every feature with an unused sketch (T9.10). (3) Holes start where the line through each point, along the sketch normal, meets the picked face, and go in along the face normal there; without a face they start on the sketch plane and go against its normal. On a curved face the points lie on the default plane that faces the first click best, and the head of each hole is carried up by its largest radius so it cuts cleanly over the curve. (4) Kernel history does not report the faces made by profile edges that end on the axis (bottom, tip, top); those faces are named by their height along the axis.
Status: Default
Reason: The spec wants a position sketch owned by the feature; sketch mode cannot edit data inside another feature yet.

D313: Hole types and geometry (PHASE4_SPEC P4.1 item 2). (1) Slot versions of the hole types are left out (the spec marks them Later). (2) Bottom: flat by default (best for printing), or a drill point with a set angle (118 degrees by default). (3) A hex nut trap is a hexagonal pocket of the nut height at the face over a clearance hole; a captive nut slot is the same hexagon and a slot of the nut width at a set depth below the face, running out to a set length, over a clearance hole. A corner of the hexagon points along the slot so the nut slides in. (4) The far side countersink applies to Through All holes and sits where the hole axis leaves the part. (5) All holes of a feature are cut in one boolean (CLAUDE.md 5A.5).
Status: Default
Reason: Offer only what OpenCascade does reliably and what the spec asks for now.

D314: Cosmetic threads (PHASE4_SPEC P4.2). (1) Type `cosmetic_thread` on one round edge; it finds the cylindrical face at the edge, which side is material (hole or shaft) and which way along the axis the face runs. It makes no geometry. Every feature result can carry thread marks (start, axis, major diameter, pitch, length, face diameter, internal); tapped holes with Cosmetic Thread ticked make one per hole. (2) Display: rings at every pitch (at most 40 per thread) drawn one percent off the face, inside a hole or outside a shaft so the shaded part does not cover them, with the sketch lines. The rings are made in the rebuild worker. (3) STEP: AP214 and AP242 as written by the kernel's plain STEP writer have no thread entity, so each thread is added as one line of the file's FILE_DESCRIPTION (size, internal or external, major diameter, pitch, length, start and axis). Readers keep it and ignore it for geometry.
Status: Default
Reason: The spec asks for metadata in STEP where the format allows; the description is the one place every STEP reader keeps.

D315: Modelled threads (PHASE4_SPEC P4.3). (1) The helix is exact (a line on a cylindrical surface) and the profile is swept along it with the kernel's corrected Frenet frame. The fixed binormal mode was tried first: it builds a valid looking solid that the booleans then mishandle (wrong volumes), so it is not used. (2) Profile: the nominal 60 degree V of ISO 68 and ANSI B1.1 with sharp roots. Cut threads are V grooves whose flanks match the basic profile (external root at the sharp V, internal groove to the major diameter plus H/8); extruded threads are ridges with the basic crest flat (P/8 on shafts, P/4 in holes) standing on the face. Profiles reach 5 percent of the pitch past the face so the booleans meet cleanly; a profile wider than the pitch, a shaft smaller than the root or a hole larger than the thread is an error that says what to change. (3) Cut threads start one pitch before the start edge so the groove runs out of the open end; extruded threads start at the edge. (4) Multiple starts are copies turned evenly about the axis with a lead of starts times pitch. At most 400 turns, to keep rebuilds reasonable. (5) Left out: a separate start reference (the start edge with an offset covers it), profile mirror and rotate (the V profile is symmetric, so both change nothing), and Up to Selection with a straight edge (vertices, flat faces and planes are offered). Profiles are nominal; the panel says so instead of a tree warning, so a working thread does not show yellow.
Status: Default
Reason: Offer only what OpenCascade does reliably; volumes are checked against Pappus sums in the tests.

D316: Fastening placement and the mounting boss (PHASE4_SPEC P4.4 item 1). (1) A position is a picked vertex, the centre of a round edge, a sketch point, or typed X, Y and Z set by clicking on the face; the point is moved onto the face along the direction (or the face normal), and the feature grows along the direction or the normal there. (2) On a curved face the base reaches down until it meets the face under the whole outline (checked along the outline), so the boss and fins join the face everywhere. (3) Head side has the counterbore at the top of the boss with the clearance hole below it; thread side has a plain hole from the top (for a self tapping screw, a tap or an insert). Pin type puts a pin on top; pin hole cuts the matching hole. (4) Fins start on the boss axis and reach the fin length beyond the boss side; the end chamfer cuts the top outer corner by a distance and angle; fin draft leans both fin sides. Not equally spaced fins step by the difference between the first and second fin angles. (5) Picking a sketch point in the 3D view is left out (sketches are not pickable in the view); a sketch point works when stored, and a vertex, round edge or click covers placement.
Status: Default
Reason: PHASE4_SPEC P4.4 item 1 in own words, using only operations OpenCascade does reliably.

D317: Snap hook and groove (PHASE4_SPEC P4.4 items 2 and 3). (1) The hook is one prism of a side outline in the plane of the up and hook directions, centred on the position across its width: a beam tapering from the base depth to the top depth, a catch ledge, the lip front, a lead in slope at the top draft from the up direction, and the top. A slope that would pass the back of the hook is an error. (2) The groove outline follows the hook head (catch, lip front and the lead in slope, so a drafted hook gets a drafted groove), grown by the groove clearance in front and the gap clearance behind, with the gap height above the head and the offset width on each side; the offset height lowers its ledge below the catch. (3) The groove is cut only from the solid that has the picked body face, never from the hook's own body. The hook height of the groove defaults to the hook's.
Status: Default
Reason: The spec lists the values; their exact geometric meaning is ours.

D318: Lip and groove (PHASE4_SPEC P4.4 item 4). (1) Picks are flat rim faces round an opening (the top of a shelled part). The lip is a band along the opening's edge, the lip width wide, standing up by the lip height; the groove is a band along the opening's edge of its rim, cut down by the groove height. Corners of the band are rounded (an offset with arcs). A band wider than the wall is an error. (2) Link matched values: groove width is lip width plus spacing, groove depth is lip height plus gap, groove draft equals lip draft. (3) Left out for now: picking edges instead of faces and tangent propagation along them, Jump gaps and Keep existing wall faces (the band always follows the inner edge of the rim). A drafted band leans both walls toward its middle.
Status: Default
Reason: Offer what OpenCascade does reliably; the left out options need edge chain following that is not built yet.

D319: Vent (PHASE4_SPEC P4.4 item 5). (1) The sketch curves get roles in a table (boundary, rib, spar, fill in boundary) because sketch curves cannot be picked in the 3D view. (2) The opening is cut through the wall under the boundary (to where a line down from the opening leaves the part). Ribs and spars are strips of their width along sketch lines, clipped to the opening, from their offset below the face down by their depth (at most the wall). The fill in is the fill boundary clipped to the opening. Spars need a rib; the fill in must be crossed by a rib. (3) The total area is the boundary area; the open area is it minus everything ribs, spars and fill cover (overlaps counted once). They are worked out in the preview job and shown in the panel as it updates. (4) Left out for now: vents on curved faces, draft on the vent walls and the fillet at the joins.
Status: Default
Reason: Offer what OpenCascade does reliably and record what is left out.

D320: Rib (PHASE4_SPEC P4.5). (1) The open chain is carried on past both ends (Linear: straight on; Natural: an end arc keeps curving, short of a full turn), then swept far toward the part: in the sketch plane square to the chain's chord (Parallel to Sketch, thickness out of the plane) or straight out of the plane (Normal to Sketch, thickness across the curve). The swept shape is cut down to the empty space round the part and the piece that holds the sketch curve is kept, so the rib stops wherever it meets the part. A piece that runs out to the far box means the rib does not meet the part on every side: an error. (2) When only the other side of the curve meets the part, the rib grows that way unless Flip is ticked. (3) Normal to Sketch on curves thickens the rib's mid surface on each side with the kernel's simple thicken; the kernel can return that solid inside out, so it is turned round when its volume is negative, and the side is checked with a point. (4) Draft is offered for Normal to Sketch ribs from one straight line (an exact prism); an inward draft limits how far the rib can grow, and a rib that would close before meeting the part is an error. Left out: draft for Parallel to Sketch and for curved chains, and thickness measured at the wall (thickness is always at the sketch plane).
Status: Default
Reason: Offer only what OpenCascade does reliably and record what is left out.

D321: Dome (PHASE4_SPEC P4.6). (1) Flat faces only. A round face (one full circle) gets a spherical cap through its rim with the distance as height, or with Elliptical a half ellipsoid of that height; distance 0 gives a half sphere or ellipsoid tangent to the side. (2) A polygon face with Continuous gets the face pushed up and cut by one sphere through its farthest rim point and the top over its centre (the dome's sides rise from the face edges where the sphere is above them). Without Continuous each straight edge gets a cylinder through that edge and the top, and the dome is what all of them leave: it rises from every edge. A curved edge needs Continuous. (3) Reverse mirrors the dome into the part and cuts it. (4) Left out for now: domes on curved faces, the constraint sketch of points, and the direction option (the dome always rises square to the face).
Status: Default
Reason: Offer only what OpenCascade does reliably and record what is left out.

D322: Wrap, analytical method (PHASE4_SPEC P4.7, PLAN Phase 4). (1) Cylindrical and flat faces, as PLAN says; cones and general extruded faces are left out for now, and the Spline surface method is Later in the spec. (2) On a cylinder the sketch plane must be parallel to the axis and touch the cylinder (within 0.0001 mm). Each sketch curve is laid in the plane as a 2D curve across and along the touching line, made an exact rational B-spline, and its poles are scaled across by one over the radius into the cylinder's angle and height, so lengths along the surface match the sketch. The wrapped face is made thick outward (emboss, fused) or inward (deboss, cut) with the kernel's simple thicken, checked by where its centre lies. (3) Scribe splits the part's faces along the wrapped outlines: the volume stays the same and the face gets new edges. (4) Reverse wraps the sketch the other way round the axis (as seen from inside). The optional pull direction for emboss and deboss is left out: material always grows square to the face.
Status: Default
Reason: An exact mapping that OpenCascade handles reliably.

D323: Sketch text (PHASE4_SPEC P4.8). (1) Glyph outlines come from the kernel's font support (FreeType inside OpenCascade, already a dependency) using the installed system fonts; no font file is bundled, so no new dependency or license. A font that is not installed is an error naming it. (2) Text is a list of text items in the sketch data, not a sketch entity: it takes no relations or dimensions, and its glyphs join the sketch profile as closed faces (a sketch with only text is a profile of the text). The 3D view draws text outlines with the sketch lines. (3) Layout: each character is placed by its advance times the spacing percent, scaled across by the width factor, turned by its own angle and then by the base line direction. Along a line or arc the text runs in the curve's direction with its top to the left of it; Full spreads the characters over the curve length or the text box width. Flip horizontal mirrors about the start square to the base line (reads backward), flip vertical mirrors about the base line. (4) The Text command opens a dialog for the open sketch; OK is one undoable sketch change. Left out for now: drawing the text inside the sketch canvas while the sketch is open (it shows in the 3D view after Exit Sketch), picking the curve in the view (it is chosen by name), and dragging the text.
Status: Default
Reason: Uses only what the kernel already ships; keeps the sketch model change small while other sessions build sketch tools.

D330: Sheet Metal folder (PHASE5_SPEC P5.1 item 1). A feature of type `sheet_metal` holds the part's defaults and sits just below the default planes. Every sheet metal feature refers to it with `refs.sheet_metal`, so editing it rebuilds them all through the usual dependency keys. Thickness is part wide and lives only in the folder. The spec's "sheet parameters on the Base Flange panel become the part defaults" is met by asking for them first: starting Base Flange in a part with no folder adds the folder (one undoable step) and opens its panel; OK there opens the Base Flange panel. Later Base Flanges and the other features may override the radius and bend allowance with their own values.
Status: Default
Reason: One place for the defaults keeps "edit the folder, update every feature" simple, and the file format stays additive.

D331: Sheet metal defaults. K-factor 0.44 (the spec asks for it in place of 0.5), thickness 1 mm, inside bend radius 1 mm, rectangular relief with ratio 0.5 of the thickness. Edge flange: 90 degrees, length from the outer virtual sharp, material inside, Trim Side Bends on and gap 1 mm in the panel. Tick box settings are stored only when on, as the shared forms do, so Trim Side Bends, Show Bend Lines and Show Bounding Box are off when the key is missing from a file and the panel starts them on.
Status: Default
Reason: The spec names the K-factor; the other values are round numbers that suit thin printed or cut sheet.

D332: Bend table (P5.1 item 2). Stored as CSV text in the folder's top level `bend_table` key, one row per thickness (mm), radius (mm), angle (degrees) and allowance (mm), with an optional header row. A bend uses the rows with the same thickness and radius (within 0.000001 mm) and interpolates linearly in angle; an angle outside the rows, or no rows, is an error that says what to add. No extrapolation. The Bend allowance method uses its typed length for every bend; Bend deduction gives BA = 2 x (R + T) x tan(A / 2) - BD.
Status: Default
Reason: Plain data in the file (opening a file never runs code), exact for the angles the shop measured, and never a silent guess.

D333: Sheet model (P5.2 to P5.5). A sheet metal part is held as a tree of flat walls joined by bends (`fdcad/core/features/sheetmetal/model.py`). Each wall is a plate in its own frame between z = 0 and the thickness; each bend joins a line on its parent's z = 0 face to its child wall. The same data builds the folded part (bends as turned rectangles) and the flat pattern (bends as strips one bend allowance wide), so flat lengths are exact for the chosen method. Each sheet metal feature copies the model from the last sheet metal result, changes it and rebuilds the part in one fuse. A part only flattens while every body change after the Base Flange comes from sheet metal features (PLAN limit).
Status: Default
Reason: Unfolding a general solid is much harder and less exact; the PLAN limits flattening to parts made from these features, which this model covers exactly.

D334: Base Flange profiles (P5.2 item 1). Closed: the profile is a plate thickened along the sketch normal (Reverse: to the other side; Symmetric: half each side). Open: the profile is one chain of lines and arcs that starts and ends with a line. The sketch is one face of the sheet: by default the material lies on the left of the chain's travel (from its free end with the smallest coordinates), Flip Side puts it on the right, Symmetric centres it. Sharp corners become bends of the default inside radius on the inside of the turn; an arc becomes a bend whose sketch side face follows the arc, so its inside radius is the arc radius less the thickness on that side. The From list and the end conditions are the ones of Extrude, but the start and end must be parallel to the sketch plane, since walls are flat plates.
Status: Default
Reason: The spec says what the profile becomes but not which side the sheet grows on or how arcs size the bend.

D335: Edge Flange position and length (P5.3 items 4 and 5). With R the inside radius, T the thickness and A the bend angle, the bend's tangent line sits inside the picked edge by: material inside R + T, material outside R, bend outside 0, virtual sharp (R + T) x tan(A / 2) (the outer virtual sharp lands on the edge). The flat wall length is the typed length less (R + T) x tan(A / 2) from the outer virtual sharp, less R x tan(A / 2) from the inner virtual sharp, or the typed length from the bend tangent. Picking an edge on the z = thickness face bends toward that face; Reverse bends the other way. Angle mode Parallel or Perpendicular sets the angle from a picked flat face. Up to Vertex ends the wall on the plane through the vertex square to the wall, or on the plane through it parallel to the base. Angles must be between 0 and 180 degrees.
Status: Default
Reason: The spec lists the options without the setbacks; these are the standard sheet metal relations, written so every option gives a different, predictable result.

D336: Reliefs and neighbouring flanges (P5.1 item 3, P5.3 item 2). When two picked edges of one Edge Flange share a corner, each flange is shortened there by the other's tangent setback plus the gap (Trim Side Bends on), or by half the gap (off; the flanges may then overlap and the Flat Pattern warns). Where a bend stops short of its edge a relief is cut: rectangular or obround (round inner end), width and depth from the ratio times the thickness, or typed sizes, reaching the depth past the tangent line; tear is a 0.02 mm slit with no depth. The rest of the corner out to the old edge is cleared down to the tangent line, so no loose tab is left. Flanges on edges of earlier flanges are not trimmed against them.
Status: Default
Reason: The spec names the relief types and sizes but not where the corner material goes; this keeps every result one valid solid.

D337: Multi length (P5.3 item 4). The first picked edge uses `length`; the 2nd to 8th edges may have their own `length2` to `length8`, shown in the panel once that many edges are picked. In the view each flange gets a length drag handle with its clickable value label (D148), which is the per edge length label the spec asks for. Edges after the 8th use `length`.
Status: Default
Reason: The shared form layout is static; eight own lengths cover normal parts and the handles reuse existing viewport work.

D338: Sketched Bend (P5.4). The sketch holds exactly one line on a flat face of the sheet; the line is extended across the whole wall. On the first wall the larger side stays fixed and Flip Fixed Side keeps the other; on any other wall the side joined to the rest of the sheet stays fixed (Flip is an error there). With the line at d across it and BA the bend allowance: centreline puts the bend strip from d - BA/2 to d + BA/2, material inside from d - BA to d, material outside from d to d + BA, and bend outside starts the bend at d and keeps the full length of the moved side (the flat pattern grows by BA). Faces of the moved side are renamed `<fid>/moved/<old name>`. Flanges already on the moved side move with it; a line through another bend is an error.
Status: Default
Reason: The spec lists the positions without numbers; the first three keep the flat pattern unchanged, as a bend drawn on a flat sheet should.

D339: Flat Pattern (P5.5 items 1 to 4, 7). Type `flatten` (the name FDEF_SPEC 5.3 planned). It is always last: while it is off, new features are inserted above it (`rollback.insert_index`); while it is on, new features go below it and apply to the flat state only, and they are skipped with a warning while the part is folded (rebuild engine). Bend lines are drawn as edges in the view and can be hidden. Overlap: pieces of the flat pattern that share volume give a warning naming the feature whose piece overlaps, with its faces highlighted. A part with another feature after its last sheet metal feature shows a warning naming it (an error while Flatten is on). Grain direction is an edge of the first wall; the panel's box is the flat pattern's size along and across it.
Status: Default
Reason: The spec gives the behaviour; these are the storage and engine choices that make it work with the existing tree and rebuild.

D340: Flat pattern export (P5.5 item 5). STEP writes the flat solid. DXF (R12 ASCII, millimetres) and SVG (1 user unit = 1 mm, sizes in mm) draw the flat pattern seen from the z = thickness face of the first wall, in that wall's frame: layers `OUTLINE`, `BEND_LINES` and the optional `BOUNDING_BOX`. Lines and circular arcs are written exactly; other curves as short lines within 0.01 mm. SVG bend lines are dashed and carry "Bend up 90 degrees" style titles.
Status: Default
Reason: True scale and separate layers are what laser and water jet software need; R12 opens almost everywhere.

D341: Sheet Metal tab and panels (PHASE5_SPEC P5.1 to P5.5, PLAN section 8 item 1). A Sheet Metal command tab sits between Sketch and Evaluate with Base Flange, Edge Flange, Sketched Bend, Sheet Metal Parameters, Load Bend Table, Flatten and Export Flat Pattern; the commands are in the shortcut editor's Sheet Metal group with no default keys, and in the Insert menu. Command ids follow the existing `feature.<type>` form (`feature.base_flange`, `feature.sheet_metal` for the parameters, `feature.flatten`, `feature.bend_table`) and `file.export_flat`. The panels use the shared Phase 3 form tables, so edits are one undoable step; Own Bend Values and Own Relief are tick groups whose fields are written only while ticked. When the first Base Flange is accepted, a Flat Pattern is added at the end of the tree as its own undoable step. Flatten flips the Flat Pattern's `flattened` setting (one undoable step, adding the Flat Pattern when it is missing). Load Bend Table reads a CSV file, checks it and stores it in the folder with the Bend table method. The Flat Pattern panel shows the flat size (length along the grain by width). Bend lines are drawn with the sketch curves while the part is flat. Export Flat Pattern picks STEP, DXF or SVG from the file name or filter and writes it on the thread pool.
Status: Default
Reason: Reuses the shared form and command code, so the shared registries change only by small additions.

D342: build123d script export (PLAN Phase 5). File, Export, build123d Script writes a Python script that uses the build123d library; FDCAD never runs it and build123d is not a dependency (the script is plain text). The script places every sketch on its plane written out in full (origin, x and z directions as the rebuild placed it), so sketches on faces land correctly. Closed chains of lines and arcs become faces; a chain or circle inside an odd number of other chains is subtracted. Extrude (Blind, Mid Plane, Two Directions; Through All as a long extrude) and Revolve (one direction about a sketch line) are written as code; every other feature type, option (From list, draft, thin, Cut Outside, Selected Regions, other end conditions), and every feature that is rolled back or failed is written as a comment that says what was left out. Global variables are listed as comments; dimensions are written as their values.
Status: Default
Reason: PLAN asks for a one way export with unsupported items as comments; writing the plane in full avoids guessing how build123d names planes.

D400: One background kernel job at a time. Previews, rebuilds, measuring, region and outline jobs ran on Qt's global thread pool at the same time and shared the last rebuild's shapes. OpenCascade can write to a shape while reading it (meshing, naming), and an intermittent access violation showed up in the full test run (rib panel accept while a preview ran). Every QRunnable that calls the kernel now decorates `run` with `fdcad.core.kernel.kernel_job`, which holds the re-entrant `KERNEL_LOCK`. The UI thread never takes the lock, so it never blocks; a preview simply waits for a running rebuild. The kernel's own parallel modes (PLAN 11.3) run inside one job and stay on.
Status: Default
Reason: Shapes are shared between jobs by design (D109 previews reuse the last rebuild's results). Serialising the jobs is the smallest change that removes the race without copying shapes.


D350: DXF and SVG export of a flat face or a sketch (PLAN Phase 2). (1) File, Export, Export DXF and Export SVG take one flat face picked in the 3D view, else the sketch selected in the feature tree. Construction curves and points of a sketch are left out. (2) The edges are moved into the plane's own coordinates (the sketch plane, or the face's plane seen from outside the part, so a bottom face is not mirrored) and written at true size in the part's units: millimetres, or inches for inch parts (values divided by 25.4). (3) DXF is plain ASCII with R12 entities (LINE, CIRCLE, ARC, POLYLINE) on layer 0 and `$INSUNITS` 4 (mm) or 1 (in) in the header. SVG carries the unit in its width and height (for example `width="100mm"`), one user unit is one part unit, Y is mirrored so the drawing is not upside down, strokes are black and 0.1 mm wide (0.004 in) with no fill. (4) Lines, circles and arcs are exact; any other curve (spline, ellipse) becomes a polyline within 0.01 mm, at most 2000 points per curve, so a single curve never becomes a large point set (CLAUDE.md 5A rule 2). (5) A curved face or an empty selection gives a message that says what to pick. Golden files are in `tests/golden/flat`.
Status: Default
Reason: PLAN gives the formats and true scale but not the source picks, the DXF version or how curves other than arcs are written. R12 entities open in every common DXF reader and polylines keep the export simple.

D351: Printer profiles and material densities (PLAN section 8 item 16). (1) A profile has a name, build volume X, Y and Z, nozzle diameter, overhang angle, minimum wall, fit tolerance and slicer path. It is a frozen `PrinterProfile` in `core/printing/profiles.py` with plain dictionary storage, so `core` stays free of Qt. (2) Profiles are application preferences, not part data: they are stored as JSON under `printing/profiles` with the active profile's name under `printing/active`, and the file format does not change. There is always at least one profile; the default is the generic printer of PLAN 8 item 16 (220 by 220 by 250 mm, 0.4 mm nozzle, 45 degree overhang, 0.8 mm minimum wall, 0.2 mm fit tolerance, the system's default app for 3MF files). Names are kept unique by adding a number. (3) A new Printing page in Preferences picks, adds (a copy of the current one), removes (never the last) and edits profiles, and holds the material density table with a reset button. (4) Density presets in g/cm3, typical values for solid material: PLA 1.24, PETG 1.27, ABS 1.04, ASA 1.07, TPU 1.21, Resin 1.15. Users can change them and add their own rows; they are stored under `printing/densities`. (5) The print tools use the active profile; Split for Printing keeps its own panel values (D293) and is left unchanged here to avoid conflicts with other work.
Status: Default
Reason: PLAN lists the profile fields and the default printer but not where profiles live or the density values. Keeping them in the preferences means a part opens the same on every machine.

D352: Open in Slicer (PLAN Phase 2). (1) A command in the File menu and the Evaluate tab's Print group. The part is written as 3MF (the same writer and mesh settings as File, Export, in the print orientation of D353) to `<system temp>/fdcad-slicer/<part name>.3mf` in the background; sending again overwrites the same file, so temporary files do not pile up. The file is left for the slicer to read. (2) With no slicer set in the active profile the system's default app for 3MF files opens it (`os.startfile` on Windows, `open` on macOS, `xdg-open` elsewhere). A set slicer is started as `program file`; a macOS `.app` bundle is started with `open -a`. FDCAD does not wait for it. (3) A slicer path that does not exist, or a start that fails, gives a status bar message pointing to Preferences, Printing. No network access is involved (CLAUDE.md rule 8).
Status: Default
Reason: PLAN gives the behaviour; these are the platform details. Reusing one temporary file per part keeps the temporary folder clean without deleting a file the slicer may still read.

D353: Print orientation and the build volume check (PLAN Phase 2, FDEF_SPEC section 2 item 11). (1) Lay Face Flat (Evaluate tab, Print group) uses the one picked face, or waits for the next face picked in the 3D view. Only a flat face with a stable name is taken; it is stored as a face reference in `print_setup.down_face` by one undoable command, which redraws but does not rebuild (the solid does not change). Clear Print Orientation sets it back to `null`. The schema does not change: the key already existed. (2) Laying flat turns the part by the shortest turn that points the face's outward normal straight down, then moves it so its lowest point is at Z 0 and its box is centred on the bed. Turning about the vertical is not changed. (3) STL, 3MF and Open in Slicer export that moved copy; STEP stays in model coordinates because it is a CAD exchange file, not a print file. With no face laid flat every export is unchanged from before. A face that can no longer be found or is no longer flat exports the part as modelled with a status bar note. (4) Build Volume is an on and off overlay: the bed (a see through face) and the volume's twelve edges of the active profile are drawn back in model coordinates under the part as it would print, green when it fits and red when not, and worked out again in the background after each rebuild, orientation change or tab change. The status bar gives the part's size on the bed, the build volume and the axes that are too large, and suggests laying another face flat, scaling or Split for Printing. (5) The overlays draw on top of the kernel view through a small helper (`ui/print_tools/overlay.py`) so the viewport module is not changed.
Status: Default
Reason: PLAN says orientation affects export only. Keeping STEP in model coordinates avoids surprising CAD users; the shortest turn keeps the part's other directions as modelled.

D354: Overhang analysis (PLAN Phase 2). (1) Overhang Analysis is an on and off overlay in the Evaluate tab's Print group. The build direction is the print orientation's up direction (D353), else +Z; the angle is the active profile's overhang angle (D351, default 45 degrees). (2) A piece of surface overhangs when it leans more than that angle away from the build direction, that is when its outward normal points down along the build direction by more than the sine of the angle. Vertical walls never overhang; surface lying at the lowest height (on the bed) is supported and never counts. (3) The part is triangulated with the display mesh settings, so the shown part's mesh is reused, and the kernel writes it once as binary STL; every triangle is tested in one numpy pass and areas are summed per face with `numpy.bincount`. The triangle count of each face (faces in explorer order, as the kernel writes them) gives the face of each triangle. (4) A face is painted red when at least 90 percent of its area overhangs and orange when at least 2 percent does (a round face lying on its side is partly overhanging), and is left alone below that. The colours are painted over the part's own colours and taken off when the overlay is turned off; it is worked out again after each rebuild, orientation change or tab change.
Status: Default
Reason: PLAN asks for colouring faces; a per face share keeps curved faces honest without drawing a separate mesh. Two colours separate a face that needs support everywhere from one that needs it only along part of it.

D355: Volume and print weight estimate (PLAN Phase 2). (1) Print Estimate (Evaluate tab, Print group) opens a small tool window that stays open: Material (the presets and user rows of D351), Density, Bodies, Volume and Weight, with the note that it is a solid part estimate and that the slicer gives the real figure with its walls and infill. (2) The bodies are those holding any face, edge or vertex picked in the 3D view, else every body of the part. The volume is the kernel's exact volume of each body, worked out in the background when the window opens and after every rebuild while it is open; changing the material or density only multiplies, with no kernel work. (3) Volume shows in cm3 for millimetre parts and in3 for inch parts; weight in grams with one decimal. (4) Editing the density in the window changes that material's preset in the preferences (presets are editable, PLAN), and the material picked last is remembered.
Status: Default
Reason: PLAN gives the formula and the label; these are the display details. Cubic centimetres read better than cubic millimetres for printed parts.

D356: Geometry check tool (PLAN section 5A item 10). (1) Geometry Check (Evaluate tab, Check group) opens a tool window that checks every body of the part in the background, including imported STEP bodies and open shells, and lists what it finds; clicking a row highlights that face or edge in the 3D view with the errors panel's highlight. Nothing is repaired (CLAUDE.md rule 12); each message says what to do. (2) Checks, per face and per edge (topology loops only, no mesh): invalid face (the kernel's shape analyser rejects it), sliver face (width, estimated as twice the area over the perimeter, below 0.01 mm), tiny edge (length below 0.01 mm, degenerate edges skipped), and gap (an edge whose tolerance is above 0.01 mm, which means it bridges a gap between its faces, or an open edge used by only one face; a seam counts twice, so closed round faces are fine). A body whose faces are all valid but which is invalid as a whole gets one general row. (3) The sliver and tiny edge limits can be changed in the window for the next run. The list is sorted by body, then invalid, gap, sliver and tiny edge, and capped at 200 rows. (4) With the pre checks and edge by edge pinpointing already built for fillets and shells (D213, D217), this completes the PLAN Phase 2 robustness line.
Status: Default
Reason: PLAN names the four problem kinds but not the limits or how a gap is found. Edge tolerance and open edges are what the kernel itself uses to describe gaps, so the check needs no extra geometry work.

D357: Phase 2 sample parts (PLAN Phase 2, D78). Built in code in `samples/parts_phase2.py`, fully defined, saved by `python -m fdcad.samples.make` with golden results; the earlier samples and their golden values are unchanged. (1) `enclosure`: an 80 by 60 by 40 mm box with its four upright edges rounded at 8 mm, the bottom outline rounded at 3 mm (one picked edge; the kernel carries the round along the tangent chain) and shelled to 2 mm walls with the top face removed. (2) `lofted_handle`: a 100 mm grip lofted from a 24 by 16 mm rectangle on the Front plane to a 20 mm circle on the top face of an 8 mm core rod, so the loft merges into one body. Reference planes are being reworked in another package, so the far profile sits on a face instead of an offset plane. (3) `swept_spring`: a 2 mm round wire swept along a helix of 20 mm diameter, 6 mm pitch and 5 turns.
Status: Default
Reason: PLAN names the three samples but not their sizes. Each one uses the Phase 2 features its name promises and stays fast to rebuild.

D370: Graph storage and schema (FDEF_SPEC 12A, D27). The reader accepts schema 2; `migrate_1_to_2` adds an empty `graphs` list. A part is written as schema 2 only when it has at least one graph; a part without graphs is still written as schema 1 with no `graphs` key, byte for byte as before, and its cache key is unchanged (the key only gains `graphs` when the part has them). Graphs live in `Document.graphs` as `fdcad.core.graph.model.Graph` objects. Group ids are `k` plus a number from the graph's `next_node` counter. A `position` of null, or one naming a deleted feature, means the end of the tree.
Status: Default
Reason: D27 asks for schema 2 so older versions refuse graph files; keeping graph free parts at schema 1 means every existing file and test opens and saves unchanged.

D371: Graph engine (PLAN Phase 7, `fdcad/core/graph/engine.py`). (1) Values are plain Python data: floats in mm and radians, booleans, `(x, y, z)` tuples, a `Plane` dataclass, kernel shapes, and lists nested at most two deep. (2) Wiring rules: number, length and angle mix freely; point and vector mix; curve and body mix (both are shapes; the receiving node checks); a boolean may feed a number; anything may feed a list input and a list may feed any input. A list given to an input that takes one value runs the node once per item (longest list wins, shorter lists repeat their last item). Several wires into one input make one list in wire order. (3) Lazy evaluation: every node result is cached under a hash of the node type, its settings, the part data it reads (`env_key`), the graph seed, its id and the keys of the results wired into it. An edit therefore recomputes only the edited node and nodes downstream of it; moving a node recomputes nothing. One shared evaluator (LRU of 4000 node results) serves the rebuild and the editor. (4) Errors stay on their node; dependent nodes show "comes from a node with an error" and remember the node where it began, so features can name it. Kernel exceptions become node errors. (5) Loops are refused when wiring; a file with a loop opens and the nodes on it show an error. (6) The background worker (`worker.py`, a single thread, no Qt) evaluates a copy of the graph; a new request cancels the running one, checked between nodes and between list items.
Status: Default
Reason: PLAN Phase 7 items 1 and 10; the same content key idea as the rebuild engine (D71) keeps one mechanism for laziness.

D372: Graph outputs and the cycle rule in the rebuild (PLAN Phase 7, D26, `fdcad/core/graph/drive.py`). The rebuild runs each graph that has set variable or set feature parameter nodes just before the first feature below its position, reading only features at or above it. A driven variable is replaced by its value (typed as `<value>mm`, `rad` or a plain number) and the variables that use it are worked out again; then every typed value is refreshed as `refresh_values` does, and driven feature parameters get their value. The typed text in the part never changes, so removing the graph returns the part to the typed values. The cycle rule is checked before the rebuild: a feature at or above a graph's position that uses a driven variable (directly or through other variables, in its parameters or sketch dimensions), or whose parameter the graph sets, or a `graph_body` feature that uses the graph, is shown as an error with a message naming both and saying to move the graph; it is skipped like any failed feature. A driven parameter on such a feature is not applied.
Status: Default
Reason: Driving values like a variable change keeps one way of updating values and keeps the file's typed text the user's own.

D373: The `graph_body` feature (D23, FDEF_SPEC 12A item 7). The operation is the `operation` setting of the Add as Feature node (`new`, `add`, `subtract`), as in the FDEF_SPEC example, so the feature has no params of its own. New keeps the graph body as its own body; add and subtract use the same fuse and cut as extrude with the fuzzy tolerance (D47). Faces are named `<feature>/face/<k>` in face order. To cache it correctly the feature interface gains `key_data(feature, doc, results)` (None by default); the rebuild engine adds it to the feature's key. Graph body returns the graph's JSON, the result keys of the features above the graph and the variable values.
Status: Default
Reason: The graph is outside the feature's own entry, so its content must be part of the feature's key.

D374: Node library choices (PLAN Phase 7 items 3 to 8). Besides the listed nodes the library has a Plane node (origin and normal) and a Vector node, since plane and vector ports need a source, and a Comment node (a note with no ports; comments are nodes so the file needs no extra key). Point is one node with X, Y and Z inputs that also serves as "construct point"; Deconstruct works on points and vectors. Arithmetic is one node with an operation setting (add, subtract, multiply, divide, power, modulo, minimum, maximum); Trigonometry likewise (sin, cos, tan and inverses). Range includes both ends; Series is start plus step times 0 to count minus 1. Random Numbers and Populate Region use numpy's PCG64 generator seeded from the graph seed, a CRC of the node id and the node's own seed. Expression takes inputs a to d, whose unit kind comes from the wired output (length, angle) or the node's `a_kind` to `d_kind` settings, plus the part's variables, and is worked out with the part's expression parser only. Move, Rotate, Scale, Mirror and Linear Array take a curve or a body; Linear Array gives a list of copies. Model Reference gives a curve (an edge, a curve or sketch feature, or a face's outer boundary), a body (the solid holding a picked face) and, for a flat face, its plane; names resolve with the feature reference resolver, and a position fallback shows as a warning on the node. Attractor gives, per point, a value from Near (at an attractor) to Far (at Radius or further), the distance, and the point pushed away from the nearest attractor by Shift times (1 minus distance over Radius); attractor curves are sampled at 200 points.
Status: Default
Reason: The smallest set that makes every PLAN item usable; one node per operation family keeps the add list short.

D375: Performance guard (PLAN Phase 7 item 12). The editor and engine support graphs of up to 500 nodes (`MAX_NODES`); adding nodes past it is refused with a message. Union, Difference, Intersection and Strut Lattice with more than 200 bodies or struts stop with a warning and a Run Anyway button; Run Anyway sets the node's `allow_many` setting through an undoable edit. All booleans on many bodies run as one kernel call. Point grids are limited to 100000 points and lattices to 20000 struts.
Status: Default
Reason: PLAN budgets; asking first avoids a frozen preview after one slider move.

D376: 2D Voronoi cells (PLAN Phase 7 item 9). Points are taken into the boundary's plane, those outside the boundary and duplicates are dropped, and each cell is the box around the boundary clipped by the half planes between its point and the others, nearest first, stopping once the next point is more than twice as far as the cell's farthest corner (numpy, no extra dependency). Gap moves every half plane back by half the gap and the boundary in by half the gap. All cells are cut to the boundary in one kernel boolean. Cells come out as closed curves, ordered by their point.
Status: Default
Reason: Exact convex cells without a new dependency; one boolean for all cells.

D377: Strut lattices (PLAN Phase 7 item 9). The bounding body's exact box is filled with cells of the given size starting at its low corner. Cubic struts run along the cell edges. Octet struts join every cell corner and face centre to its twelve nearest neighbours (the face centred cubic bonds). Each strut stops short of its nodes (1.05 radii for cubic, 1.8 for octet) and every node gets a ball (1.5 and 2.1 radii), so struts meet only balls and never each other; this keeps the single fuse more than ten times faster than crossing cylinders (measured: octet block of 240 struts 13.9 s before, 1.9 s after). The radius must stay under the size where struts would vanish (cell over 2.1 for cubic, cell times 0.71 over 3.6 for octet). The fused lattice is cut to the bounding body in one boolean.
Status: Default
Reason: Ball jointed struts are a common lattice form and keep previews fast enough for the sample.

D378: Node editor panel (PLAN Phase 7 item 2, section 8 item 18, `fdcad/ui/node_editor`). (1) A dock on the right of the window, hidden until Tools, Node Editor or the Graph command tab opens it; it follows the current part. The Graph tab holds Node Editor, Set Graph Position, Add Node, Add Comment, Group and Ungroup Nodes and Fit Graph. (2) Layout: the canvas on the left; on the right the node search (always visible; double click on empty canvas or Add Node focuses it and the chosen node goes where the user clicked) above the settings of the selected node. Nodes are FDCAD's own rounded cards with a coloured band per category and round ports coloured by type; list inputs have square ports. (3) Every edit (add, delete, move, wire, unwire, settings, group, paste, position, Run Anyway) is one `EditGraph` command holding the graph's JSON before and after; slider drags of one node merge into one undo step. Adding an Add as Feature node also adds its `graph_body` feature at the end of the tree, in the same undo step. A new wire into an input that takes one value replaces the old wire. Copy puts the nodes and the wires between them on the clipboard as JSON (`application/x-fdcad-nodes`); paste reads it as data only, with new ids, 30 units down and right. (4) Keys: Add Node Shift+A, Copy and Paste Ctrl+C and Ctrl+V, Group Ctrl+G, Ungroup Ctrl+Shift+G and Delete Nodes Backspace, all scoped to the editor so they never take keys from the rest of the app; the app's own Delete key (edit.delete) also deletes on the canvas, so default keys stay unique (SHORTCUTS.md 6). Wheel zooms about the cursor (0.15 to 3 times), middle drag or Space drag pans. (5) Preview: 120 ms after the last edit the graph runs in the graph worker thread with the part's last rebuild; the worker also meshes the ghost, then the 3D view shows the geometry outputs of the selected nodes and of nodes whose geometry feeds nothing (not Add as Feature, whose body is in the part) as a see-through accent ghost that cannot be picked. Nodes with errors get a red frame and the error as a tooltip and in the settings. (6) The graph shows in the feature tree as a row below the feature at its position; double clicking the row opens the editor. (7) The panel and the node library load the first time the editor opens (PLAN 11.3 item 8); measured startup memory is unchanged (453.7 MB against 453.5 MB before, Linux container).
Status: Default
Reason: PLAN Phase 7; keeps every edit undoable and every kernel call off the UI thread.

D379: Sample graphs (PLAN Phase 7 item 13). Four samples live in `src/fdcad/samples/graphs.py`, saved to `samples/graphs/` with their own golden file `tests/golden/graph_samples.json` (written by `uv run python -m fdcad.samples.graphs`), apart from the Phase 1 to 3 samples so they never clash with other work: a 120 by 80 by 6 mm plate with a grid of 77 holes whose radius grows from 1 mm near an attractor point to 4 mm (`attractor_plate`); a 120 by 80 by 4 mm panel with 24 seeded random Voronoi cells, 3 mm webs, cut through it (`voronoi_panel`); an L bracket whose leg lengths (variables) and width (a feature parameter) come from three sliders (`slider_bracket`); and a 30 by 30 mm base with a cubic lattice of 1.2 mm struts filling a 20 mm high block on it (`lattice_block`). Tests rebuild each twice from fresh engines to the golden volume (1 part per million), face and edge counts and box, and check the full preview of each graph runs in under 1 s (measured 0.75 s for the lattice, the slowest). STEP export of the lattice reimports within 1 part in 10000 (the ball and strut joints lose a little through STEP); the others within 1 part per million.
Status: Default
Reason: PLAN Phase 7; values are our own.


D390: Equations manager (PHASE4_SPEC P4.10 item 1, PLAN Phase 4 and section 7). (1) The safe expression parser (`core/units/expressions.py`, still a hand written parser, never `eval`) gains, inside formulas only: quoted names (`"Width"`, `"depth@Extrude 1"`), the comparisons `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`, `==`, `!=` (result 1 or 0, compared with a tolerance of 1e-9 relative), and the functions `if(condition, then, else)`, `and`, `or`, `not`, `asin`, `acos`, `atan`, `atan2`, `floor` and `ceil`. A double quote right after a number is still the inch symbol; anywhere else it opens a quoted name, so `1' 3"` reads as before. Units stay strict inside formulas (D66): `="Width" > 40mm`, not `> 40`. (2) `core/equations` solves every typed value of the part together: global variables (by name, quoted or not), feature values (every typed parameter and sketch dimension, named `<param>@<feature name>`, for example `"depth@Extrude 1"` or `"d1@Sketch 1"`; `"depth@f6"` with the feature id also works and survives a rename) and suppression formulas. Values are evaluated in dependency order; a loop (found with Tarjan's algorithm) is a circular reference error on every value in it, values that use a failed value fail with "Uses ..., which has an error", and everything else still solves. The rebuild shows a feature whose formula cannot be solved as an error naming the value; `document_variables` now returns every name a field can use, so all value fields accept feature values. (3) The manager's three sections: Global Variables (every variable), Feature Values (features whose suppression is set by a formula: the optional feature key `suppression`, nonzero means suppressed, with the names `suppressed` and `unsuppressed` for 1 and 0), Equations (feature values whose typed text is a formula). Deleting an equation keeps the value's current number as plain text. A new variable's kind comes from its value: a unit gives a length or angle, no unit gives a plain number (which takes a field's own unit when used, D66). (4) Comments: a variable's optional `comment` key, and a feature's optional `comments` map (value name to text, `suppressed` for the suppression formula); both are left out when empty, so older files save unchanged (FDEF_SPEC 4, 5.1). (5) The manager is a non modal dialog (Tools, Equations; command `tools.equations`, no default key), so a double click on a dimension shown in the view puts its quoted name into the cell being edited instead of opening the value box. It is pure Python and runs on the UI thread: solving touches no kernel. OK applies everything as one undoable `SetEquations` command. (6) The Equations folder in the feature tree lists the global variables (shown only while the part has some, so trees of older parts are unchanged); a double click opens the manager. (7) Renaming a feature does not rewrite formulas that use its name; they then show an unknown name error until fixed, or use the id form. Rewriting them is recorded in IDEAS.md.
Status: Default
Reason: P4.10 item 1 names the sections and behaviour but not the reference grammar, storage or how feature values are named; these choices keep the parser safe, keep older files byte for byte, and let one solver serve the manager, every field and the rebuild.

D391: Configurations and file schema 2 (PHASE4_SPEC P4.10 item 2, PLAN Phase 4, FDEF_SPEC 9 and 15). (1) The features and variables in the document always hold the active configuration's values, as FDEF_SPEC 5.1 item 4 already said for `suppressed`, so the rebuild, the tree and every panel work unchanged. Each configuration stores in `overrides` its own value for every configured path (a value that differs between configurations): `<feature id>.<param>` (parameter objects, strings, booleans or numbers, so any feature value), `<sketch id>.<dimension id>` (`f5.d1`), `<feature id>.suppressed` (a boolean) and `var.<name>`. Every configuration holds every configured path; a path no configuration overrides is shared. (2) Scopes: every value field's right click menu has Configurations, This Configuration, All Configurations or Chosen Configurations, while the part has two or more configurations. All makes the value shared again; This and Chosen give the new value to those configurations and keep the old value in the others. Without a choice the default rule applies: switching first stores the live values of configured paths in the active configuration, so an edit changes only the active configuration when the path is already configured and all configurations when it is not. The feature tree menu adds Suppress (or Unsuppress) in This Configuration. A panel edit with a scope is one undo step (the edit and the scope as a macro). (3) The Configurations tab (a fifth left panel tab, Tools, Configurations; commands `tools.configurations` and `tools.design_table`, no default keys) lists the configurations with the active one in bold: Add Configuration (copies the active values and shows the new one), Show Configuration or a double click, Rename (in place) and Delete (the last one cannot be deleted; deleting the active one shows the first other). Each is one undoable command that stores the configurations block, the variables and copies of the changed features only. (4) Schema 2 (FDEF_SPEC 9, 15): each configuration's `suppressed` list is replaced by `<id>.suppressed` overrides, overrides may hold any feature value, and the active configuration's overrides equal the document's values. `migrate_1_to_2` turns each listed feature into an override in every configuration (true where listed, false elsewhere); paths that some configurations lack get the file's value. A file is written as schema 2 only when a configuration has an override or the part has a design table; otherwise it is written exactly as schema 1, so every older sample and fixture opens and saves byte for byte unchanged (tested). FDCAD reads both. On open the active configuration's overrides are written into the document, so a hand edited file stays consistent. (5) FDEF_SPEC 12A planned schema 2 for graphs (Phase 7). Schema 2 now also carries the configuration change; a schema 2 reader treats a missing `graphs` array as empty, so the node editor work can add its array to schema 2 without another version.
Status: Default
Reason: P4.10 item 2 and the task brief ask for per configuration overrides of any value and suppression with a migration. Keeping the document as the active configuration avoids touching the rebuild and every panel; writing the lowest schema that holds the data keeps older files and other sessions' byte for byte tests unchanged.

D392: Design tables (PHASE4_SPEC P4.10 item 3, PLAN Phase 4, FDEF_SPEC 9 item 4). (1) The table lives in the configurations block as FDEF_SPEC 9 planned: column paths (the same forms as configuration overrides, D391) and one row of typed text per configuration. Cells: expressions for typed values (evaluated with the part's names, so formulas work), `S` or `U` for suppression (also yes, no, true, false, 1, 0), `true` or `false` for tick box settings, the plain word for choices. An empty cell leaves that configuration's value as it is. (2) "Kept in sync by the app": the rows are rebuilt from the configurations whenever the file is written, so an edit made in a panel or in the Configurations tab shows in the table and the two never disagree. Columns that no longer name a value (a deleted feature) are dropped on save. (3) The editor (Tools, Design Table, or the Configurations tab's Design Table button; a dialog because it is a large grid) starts from the stored columns with each configuration's current values. Add Row adds a configuration, Delete Row deletes it on OK (rows are the configurations), Add Column offers every variable, feature value, sketch dimension and suppression path, Delete Column only removes the column. OK applies the whole table as one undoable command; a bad cell is refused with its row and column named and nothing changes. Remove Table drops the table and keeps the configurations. (4) CSV: a header row `Configuration,<path>,...` and one row per configuration, written with the standard library `csv` module (UTF-8, commas, quotes where needed). Import accepts a byte order mark, blank lines and short rows (missing cells are empty), and replaces the editor's table; a configuration without a row is deleted on OK, as for Delete Row.
Status: Default
Reason: P4.10 item 3 and FDEF_SPEC 9 fix the storage but not cell syntax, empty cells or how rows and configurations stay in step; rebuilding rows on save is the simplest way to keep the promise that they never disagree.

D393: Deformation features (PHASE4_SPEC P4.9, PLAN Phase 4 and 10 item 8). (1) Five feature types, `bend`, `twist`, `taper`, `stretch` and `flow`, one module each in `core/deform` (no Qt), registered with the other feature types. Common params and refs in FDEF_SPEC 5.3.33. (2) The triad is a frame whose third axis is X, Y or Z, turned by an angle (`spin`) about it; the origin is three lengths. Trim planes are two lengths along the third axis from the origin. A new feature centres the triad on the picked bodies and puts the trim planes at their ends; params left out fall back to the same automatic values. Only the region between the planes deforms; beyond the end plane the part moves rigidly with the end of the region and below the start plane it stays, so there are no gaps.
